nameStory: This tiny lichen doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name Poeltinula infernula. The genus name honors Josef Poelt, a renowned Austrian lichenologist who spent his career studying these fascinating partnerships between fungi and algae. The species name 'infernula' means 'little hellish one,' perhaps referring to its ability to survive in harsh, exposed rocky conditions.
description: Poeltinula infernula is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches directly on rock surfaces. This organism is actually a partnership between a fungus and microscopic algae living together. It creates small, grayish to brownish patches that might be easily overlooked as just discolored rock. The patches typically measure just a few millimeters to a couple centimeters across.

idTips.label: Growth form
idTips.description: Forms thin, crusty patches that seem painted directly onto rock surfaces - you can't peel it off like paper

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-brown to dark brown coloration that may appear slightly mottled or uneven

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Surface feels rough and granular when gently touched, like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches are quite small, usually less than an inch across, though multiple patches may grow near each other

idTips.label: Fruiting bodies
idTips.description: May have tiny, dark, dot-like structures (apothecia) embedded in the surface that contain spores

habitat: Found on exposed siliceous rocks (like granite or quartzite) in open, sunny locations throughout New England's mountains and rocky outcrops. Prefers acidic rock surfaces that receive plenty of direct sunlight and good air circulation. Most likely encountered on clifftops, rocky summits, or large boulder fields above treeline.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more visible as winter snow melts away from rock faces. Any reproductive structures begin to develop during moist spring conditions.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for growth when warm temperatures and occasional summer rains provide ideal conditions. Fruiting bodies are most likely to be visible now.
seasonality.fall: Continues growing slowly as temperatures cool. The lichen may appear slightly darker or more pronounced as it prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Goes dormant under snow cover but remains visible on exposed rock faces. Appears unchanged from fall, waiting for spring moisture to resume growth.

funFact: This lichen can survive being completely dried out for months, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet - it's like a tiny resurrection happening right on the rock surface every time it rains!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with simple rock stains or other small crustose lichens. The key difference is that lichens will have a slightly raised, granular texture rather than appearing as flat discoloration, and may show tiny fruiting bodies under close inspection.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species is extremely rare in our region and may represent the edge of its known range. Finding it would be a significant discovery worth documenting with photos and location data.
compareHints: Since this is the only Poeltinula species documented in New England, compare it with other small rock-dwelling lichens in the Rhizocarpaceae family. Unlike the more common map lichens (Rhizocarpon species) that often show distinctive black borders around yellow-green patches, Poeltinula infernula lacks these contrasting colors and borders. It's generally smaller and more uniformly colored than most Rhizocarpon species.
